problem:
Your own cancellation page says it plainly. Please call 1-800-343-7373 to speak with the reservation office to cancel or alter a reservation (c11). There is no online path. The reservation office runs Monday to Friday 7:00 AM to 3:00 PM Alaska Time, published on both the Summit and the Bennett product pages, so it is standing policy rather than a one-page typo (c10). The money runs on a different clock. A cancellation made up to 24 hours prior to departure receives a refund minus a $10.00 penalty per person, and if a cancellation is made within 24 hours of departure time the guest forfeits all rights to a refund (c12).

Put those two together and the shape of the problem is arithmetic rather than opinion. The refund clock runs 24 hours a day, seven days a week. The only published route to act runs 40 hours a week. A guest holding a Sunday morning departure who decides on Saturday evening that they can't travel has nowhere to put that decision. The phone rings into a closed office. By the time Monday opens, the clock has run, the fare is forfeit, and the first anyone at White Pass hears of it is a guest who is already unhappy.

Weekends are not quiet days in Skagway. Five ships were listed arriving on Sunday August 9, 2026 (c20). Weekdays are not quiet in the office either, because the Reservation Agent job description puts the same person on entering reservations into the ticketing system, answering questions via phone, email and in person regarding White Pass products, and assisting the Passenger Department with train loading, passenger transfers and crossing-guard duties (c30). The person who would take that call is often on the platform.

A smaller version of the same gap sits on the pages themselves. The cancellation policy page states the phone requirement and states no hours at all (c11). The hours live on the product pages (c10). The contact page offers a phone number, an email address, a fax and a contact form, with no hours on it (c18). A guest who wants to do the right thing inside the window can read your cancellation policy end to end and still not learn when someone will pick up.

The honest last line of this problem is that nobody at White Pass can currently say how often any of it happens. No out-of-hours contact volume, no call volume and no email volume is published or recorded anywhere we could find. That is not a criticism. It is the first thing worth fixing, because the size of this gap is the number that decides what it is worth spending on it, and right now that number does not exist.
after_state: Monday morning, the reservation office opens to a list instead of to a voicemail backlog and a guess. Every request that arrived over the weekend is sitting there with the minute it arrived written beside it in Alaska Time, and each one already shows whether that minute fell before or after that guest's own 24 hour cutoff. The agent works down a list rather than reconstructing what happened. A guest who gave up on the phone at 9pm on a Saturday has a receipt with a time on it, so the conversation on Monday is about applying your policy rather than about whose memory is right. By the season close you can answer a question nobody at White Pass can answer today, which is how many guests try to reach you when the office is shut, what they are asking for, what language they write in, and how many of them were still inside the refund window at the moment they asked.
goals: Give every out-of-hours guest request a server-written arrival time in Alaska Time, so the moment a guest asked becomes a recorded fact rather than a memory, a voicemail or an argument.

Offer a working route to act on all three channels the guest already reaches for, the website, the 1-800 line and info@wpyr.com, so a cancellation or change request never depends on the office being open at that hour.

Put one governed source behind every guest-facing sentence about the cancellation terms, the $10.00 per person penalty and the office window, so the cancellation page, the product pages and the acknowledgements all say the same approved thing.
Change the reservation agent's Monday from reconstruction to triage, without adding a single review step, drafting task or new screen to the people who are also loading trains.

Produce the four counters that do not exist today, out-of-hours contact volume, arrival time relative to the 24 hour cutoff, language mix and intent mix, as a by-product of the work the agent already does, so the decision about what to spend next rests on your numbers instead of anyone's argument.

non_goals.item: No artificial intelligence anywhere in phase one.
non_goals.reason: That is the recommendation, not a caveat attached to one. A timestamp, a clock and a queue are deterministic and can be tested exhaustively. A model on this path would add failure modes to a surface where money moves and would buy nothing the form does not already deliver.

non_goals.item: No generated answers about the cancellation policy, the 24 hour clock, the penalty or any refund outcome.
non_goals.reason: In Moffatt v. Air Canada the tribunal held the airline liable for what the chatbot on its own website said and rejected the argument that the chatbot was a separate entity (c44). Your policy carries two clauses that are opposites separated by a preposition, up to 24 hours prior and within 24 hours (c12). A paraphrase that flips those is a money misstatement on your own site. We serve your approved words verbatim with a link, or we hand off to a person.

non_goals.item: No machine translation at runtime of any policy, price or refund text into Spanish or Japanese.
non_goals.reason: You state you are actively seeking candidates who speak Spanish and Japanese fluently (c31), which is evidence the capability is wanted rather than evidence it is present. Outbound text in a language nobody on the published staff list is confirmed to read back has no review path. The policy strings and the acknowledgements are translated once by a professional human translator and version controlled as fixed strings, re-reviewed only when the policy changes.

non_goals.item: No voice agent on the 1-800 line, in this phase or as an upsell later in the season.
non_goals.reason: It was assessed and killed. The phone is the published route for the highest-stakes contact you have (c11), no call volume exists anywhere to size or evaluate it against, and eight weeks to the October 7, 2026 close would put it live at the busiest and thinnest-staffed moment of the year with no tuning window. The narrow real win on that channel is an out-of-hours greeting and a callback record, which is a phone system configuration carrying no model.

non_goals.item: No reads or writes against the ticketing system. No booking lookup, no seat release, no reference validation.
non_goals.reason: tickets.wpyr.com is a hosted third party with no published API or integration surface, and that integration can't be assessed from outside your company by anyone, including us. We capture the booking reference as an unvalidated string the guest types, which needs no vendor at all. Assuming an integration we have never seen is the classic way a project like this blows its date.

non_goals.item: No self-service cancellation or change desk in phase one.
non_goals.reason: It needs the same write access to the ticketing system. Its correct first step is not a build at all, it is a written feasibility assessment of your ticketing vendor's interface, run in the off season, with the build gated on that assessment coming back yes.

non_goals.item: Nothing in this build decides whether a guest gets their money back.
non_goals.reason: The system records when a request arrived and flags whether that time fell before or after the cutoff. The refund decision stays with your agent and your policy. The acknowledgement a guest receives confirms receipt and the arrival time and never states a refund outcome.

non_goals.item: Nothing that touches the terms, scheduling or monitoring of the represented workforce.
non_goals.reason: About 40 workers, including tour guides, announcers and workers who greet visitors as they leave their cruise ships, voted to join SMART-TD's local chapter on April 8 (c33). That is a negotiation before it is a deployment, and it is not ours to walk into.

non_goals.item: No revenue management, dynamic pricing or yield work.
non_goals.reason: No passenger count, no load factors, no trains-per-day figure and no channel split are published anywhere, so there is no demand signal to model. Amtrak's ARROW achieved 3 to 5 percent additional revenue (c43), which is a real precedent and is not a substitute for your own data. Your pricing is also negotiated with cruise lines, one of whose parent is a minority partner in the ownership group (c5), so it is a commercial relationship before it is an algorithm.

non_goals.item: No predictive maintenance on the locomotive fleet.
non_goals.reason: The entire evidence base available to us is that six 30-class engines are currently in Skagway with the seventh and eighth due in 2026 (c36). No telemetry, no failure history and no stated maintenance pain exists anywhere in what we could verify. Proposing it would be inventing a need.

non_goals.item: No shadow-mode exercise asking your reservation agent to review machine drafts during the remaining 2026 season.
non_goals.reason: It adds work to the exact person this project exists to unload, on the days five ships are in port and they are on the platform (c30, c20). The proposal would contradict its own goal. The honest version ships no model this season and lets the agent's own resolution become the record for free.

non_goals.item: We do not replace or compete with the phone.
non_goals.reason: The 1-800 line works during office hours and your guests already use it (c11, c13). We add a path only at the hours where the existing one dead ends, and the greeting on that same line points at the published window rather than away from it.

non_goals.item: We do not build, resell or take a margin on a website chat widget.
non_goals.reason: That is an off-the-shelf commodity at published list pricing of $95 to $295 a month with no fixed-term contract (c48). Buying it is a reasonable separate decision and we are not paid for it. It is complementary rather than rival, because it answers website questions and does not create a timestamped work item against the 24 hour clock and does not touch info@wpyr.com, which is where this build lives.

metrics.metric: Out-of-hours guest requests reaching the reservation office with a server-written arrival time, counted per week and split by channel across the web form, the 1-800 callback record and info@wpyr.com.
metrics.baseline: ASSUMED ABSENT, and we will not invent one. Zero are recorded today, and the true volume is unknown, because no out-of-hours contact volume, call volume or email volume is published anywhere and none is being captured. The baseline is established by measurement in the first two full weeks of live capture. It ships labelled a shoulder season sample, because Bennett closes September 12, 2026 (c17) and the Summit season carries no service dates on September 26 to 27 and October 1, 3 to 5 (c16), so a September figure describes a shoulder period and not a July peak.
metrics.target: The volume target is set jointly at the end of week two, once the baseline exists. The decision rule is agreed in writing before go live so that it can't be moved afterwards. If two full weeks of live capture return fewer than 10 out-of-hours requests in total, the gap is smaller than the published policy implies, we write that down, and we do not propose a phase two.
metrics.timeframe: Baseline at the end of week two of live capture. Target fixed at that point and reported again at the October 7, 2026 season close.

metrics.metric: Share of captured out-of-hours requests whose server-written arrival time falls before that guest's own 24 hour cutoff.
metrics.baseline: ASSUMED ABSENT. This is the single number that decides whether the build is worth extending, and nothing published anywhere allows it to be estimated, so we do not estimate it. It becomes computable on day one of capture, because the arrival time is a server write and the departure date and product are on the request. First reported at the end of week two.
metrics.target: Set once the baseline exists, with the funding gate stated in advance. Anything beyond phase one is funded only if this share is at least 25 percent across the capture period, meaning at least a quarter of out-of-hours requests were still live inside the refund window when they arrived. Below 25 percent, the honest conclusion is that the timing gap is narrower in practice than your own policy implies, and we say so in writing rather than proposing more work.
metrics.timeframe: First computed at the end of week two of live capture, final figure at the October 7, 2026 season close.

metrics.metric: Guest-facing surfaces stating the cancellation terms, the $10.00 per person penalty or the reservation office window that render from one approved source file.
metrics.baseline: MEASURED, and it is zero. Today the window of Monday to Friday 7:00 AM to 3:00 PM Alaska Time appears on the Summit and Bennett product pages (c10), the cancellation policy page states the phone requirement and carries no hours (c11), and the contact page carries the channels and no hours (c18). No single source governs any of them.
metrics.target: 100 percent. Every guest-facing surface and every acknowledgement template that states the cancellation terms, the penalty or the office window renders from the one file you signed off, and zero guest-facing sentences about policy exist that are not a verbatim span of that file. Verified by a string containment check in code, not by anyone reading the page.
metrics.timeframe: At go live, then re-checked automatically on every deploy for the life of the build.

metrics.metric: Correctness of the 24 hour boundary and penalty computation in Alaska Time, measured as pass rate on an exhaustive test set.
metrics.baseline: MEASURED, and it is not applicable today, because no computation exists. The boundary is applied by hand by a person during office hours, and there is no record of it being applied at all outside them.
metrics.target: 100 percent pass, with a single failing case blocking the release. The test set covers both sides of the 24 hour line, the $10.00 per person penalty arithmetic, the forfeiture clause, and conversion into Alaska Time from a browser or a ship clock set elsewhere. One hazard is removed by the calendar rather than by code, since the published Summit season of April 30 to October 7, 2026 (c16) sits entirely inside a single United States daylight saving period, so no transition falls within the season.
metrics.timeframe: Before go live, and re-run on every change thereafter.

phase1_must: A structured request form served from wpyr.com, with dropdowns for request type, departure date and product, a free text box, and a booking reference field captured as an unvalidated string. Served in English, Spanish and Japanese as human translated fixed strings.
A server-written arrival time in Alaska Time stamped on every request at intake, before anything else runs, and never editable afterwards by anyone including us.

A derived flag on each request showing whether that arrival time fell before or after that guest's own 24 hour cutoff. Visible to your agent as triage information, never shown to the guest as a refund outcome.

An out-of-hours greeting on 1-800-343-7373 that states the published window of Monday to Friday 7:00 AM to 3:00 PM Alaska Time and takes a callback request, producing the same timestamped record on the channel where the guest's habit already lives.
A timestamped ingest on info@wpyr.com that queues the raw message unchanged, with the original text always retained beside anything else.
One queue the reservation office works from, with the three channels labelled and the agent's own resolution recorded on each item.

One governed source file for the cancellation terms, the penalty and the office window, signed off by you, with a string containment check in code asserting that every guest-facing policy sentence is a verbatim span of it.
Acknowledgement templates, professionally human translated into Spanish and Japanese once and version controlled, that confirm receipt and the arrival time and never state a refund outcome.

The four counters exported as a plain file you own, out-of-hours contact volume, arrival time relative to the cutoff, language mix and intent mix, generated as a by-product of the agent's normal resolution at zero added workload.
An exhaustive test suite on the 24 hour boundary, the penalty arithmetic and the Alaska Time conversion, run before go live and on every change.
phase1_later: The deterministic self-service change and cancellation desk. Gated on a written feasibility assessment of your ticketing vendor's interface, run in the off season, and it becomes a build only if that comes back yes. One standing instruction rides with it for its whole life, no model is ever placed on that path in any phase for any reason.

A single classifier on unstructured inbound email and on the form's free text box, to sort and extract from messages that arrive in whatever language the guest writes. Off season build, live before the 2027 opening, trained and evaluated on labels the 2026 season produces for free. It is not scoped today because no evaluation set exists and none can be bought, so shipping it in 2026 would be a demonstration rather than a system.
Reply drafting for the reservation agent. Deferred, because acceptance for a drafting aid is agent edit distance and time to send, and neither baseline exists yet.
Booking reference validation and booking context assembly. Blocked on the same unassessed ticketing integration, not on effort.
Any outbound Spanish or Japanese beyond the fixed human translated strings. Blocked until there is a verified reader on staff who can review it.
Anything in seasonal hiring. It has the strongest outside evidence and the weakest evidence local to you, and a union constraint sits across it.

First-party post-ride feedback capture. Worth doing and not now. Every review platform returned HTTP 403 to us, so we hold zero verbatim guest messages and nobody, including you, currently has a sample of how your own guests phrase things.

An off-the-shelf tourism chat widget at published list pricing of $95 to $295 a month with no fixed-term contract and one to four weeks of vendor configuration (c48). This is a buy recommendation we are not paid for and do not implement. Two conditions are not optional, it is configured to answer only published non-money content and to hand off on anything touching cancellation, refund or price, and you go in knowing that under Moffatt the liability for what it says on your site stays with you whoever built it (c44).
need_from_you: A POLICY DECISION THAT IS YOURS ALONE, AND THE ONE ITEM THAT CHANGES WHAT THIS IS WORTH. Is an out-of-hours request timestamped before the 24 hour cutoff honoured at that timestamp? Today the phone is the only published route (c11) and the office is shut at that hour (c10), so a Saturday evening request effectively lands on Monday, after the clock. We can record the minute a guest asked, to the second, defensibly. We can't decide for you whether that minute counts. Until you answer it, this build is honest measurement rather than a change in guest outcomes, and the answer also governs what the acknowledgement is allowed to say. We need it in writing, from a named owner, before go live.

Access to info@wpyr.com, or a forwarding rule onto an address we control. This is the longest-lead item on the list and the one most likely to move the date. The email path is one of the three capture channels and it can't be built against nothing.

A named owner of the queue, with an answer for the hard day. Who works it, at what hour, and what happens when five ships are in port and that person is on the platform for train loading and crossing-guard duty (c30, c20). A queue with no named owner becomes a second inbox, which is the failure mode this build exists to end.

A configuration change on 1-800-343-7373. Whoever administers that line sets the out-of-hours greeting and the callback capture. We need the vendor name, the administrator contact and a scheduled window. We have not seen your phone system and we will not price a guess.

Sign-off on the governed policy text. The exact wording of the cancellation terms, the $10.00 per person penalty and the office window, approved by whoever owns that language at White Pass. Under Moffatt the liability for what your site says stays with you (c44), so we will not write that sentence on your behalf. We serve the one you approve, verbatim, and we check in code that nothing else ever reaches a guest.

A professional Spanish and Japanese translator, engaged once, for the policy strings and the acknowledgement templates. Your recruiting states you are actively seeking candidates fluent in Spanish and Japanese (c31), which tells us the need is real and also tells us there may be nobody on staff today who can read a translation back. Translating once by a human and freezing the strings is the safe answer. It is a real cost and a real scheduling dependency, so it belongs on this list rather than in a footnote.

Written confirmation on the union question, before anything ships. About 40 workers voted to join SMART-TD's local chapter on April 8 (c33). Reservation Agents are not among the roles that article names, which is why this build appears clear of it. Absence from a list is not proof of non-representation, so we are asking you to confirm it rather than assuming it on your behalf.

Whoever administers wpyr.com, with a deploy path. The form is served from your site and the governed policy text has to render on your cancellation page. We need the platform, the access and an agreed way to publish.

One hour a week of the reservation office's time for four weeks after go live, to look at the queue and tell us where it is wrong. Nothing else. No drafts to review, no shadow exercise, no new screen to learn. Their normal resolution is the record we want and they already produce it.

Your sell-out rate by departure, if you hold it internally. It is the number that decides which way the short-run money runs on this build, and it is not published anywhere. If you do not hold it in usable form, say so and we will design the business case without it, which is how we have written it.

risks.risk: MAKING CANCELLATION EASIER CAN COST YOU MONEY IN THE SHORT RUN, and we would rather say it than have you find it. Today, a guest who can't reach anyone inside 24 hours forfeits all rights to a refund (c12) and the railway keeps that fare. The same guest, able to act at 9pm on a Saturday, converts a forfeiture into a refund minus a $10.00 per person penalty.
risks.mitigation: The offsetting gain is reselling the seat on a ride that usually sells out in advance (c14), plus fewer disputes and less goodwill damage. Which effect is larger depends on your sell-out rate by departure, which you do not publish and we do not have. So the business case we put in front of you does NOT lean on resold seats. It clears on the things that do not depend on that unpublished number, out-of-hours contacts captured that today bounce off a closed office, agent time not spent reconstructing a weekend while a train is loading, and the decision data itself. Phase one also measures the conversion directly, because every request carries the cutoff flag, so within one season you hold the real figure for your own railway rather than our estimate. If it comes back against you, the honest move is to stop, and the policy decision above is the lever you control.

risks.risk: The volume may turn out to be small. No out-of-hours contact volume is published or recorded anywhere, so it is genuinely possible that few guests try to act outside office hours and the gap is more theoretical than the policy makes it look.
risks.mitigation: This is exactly why phase one is a measurement instrument before it is a saving, and why it is scoped as a small pilot rather than a platform. The decision rule is agreed before go live and written into the metrics above. If two full weeks of capture return fewer than 10 out-of-hours requests, we write that down and we do not propose a phase two. Losing that argument cheaply, on your numbers, is the point of running it in this order.

risks.risk: The runway is short and the sample is not your peak. Eight weeks remain to the October 7, 2026 close, and the build, the inbox access and the phone configuration all come out of those same eight weeks, so usable observation time is meaningfully shorter than the calendar suggests. Bennett closes September 12 (c17) and the Summit season carries no service dates on September 26 to 27 and October 1, 3 to 5 (c16).
risks.mitigation: Every counter ships labelled as a shoulder season sample, so nobody designs 2027 on a September mix without knowing what it is. If access or the phone change slips past mid September, the honest call is to go live for the season close as a rehearsal and treat the 2027 opening as the real baseline. Starting in April 2027 for a full clean season is also a legitimate choice, and its only cost is a year of not knowing.

risks.risk: Guests may not adopt a new path. Research on 467 German adults found booking intention significantly lower for automated agents than for human ones, with both main effects significant (c45).
risks.mitigation: That study tested a chatbot, and nothing here asks a guest to converse with a machine or to learn a new behaviour. A form with dropdowns is the most ordinary interaction on the internet, the phone greeting meets the habit exactly where it already is (c11), and the email path asks the guest to do precisely what they do today. The new route is offered at the one moment the old one dead ends. If adoption is still low, the counters say so within weeks and the finding costs you a pilot rather than a season.

risks.risk: A guest could read an acknowledgement as a promise of a refund. That is close to the Moffatt fact pattern, where the tribunal held the airline responsible for a misrepresentation made by the chatbot on its own website and rejected the separate-entity argument (c44).
risks.mitigation: The acknowledgement confirms receipt and the arrival time and never states a refund outcome, which is a hard rule rather than a style guideline. Every guest-facing sentence about policy is a verbatim span of the file you signed off, asserted by a string containment check in code rather than by anyone's judgement on the day. No model writes a word of guest-facing text in phase one. The wording is yours and you approve it before it ships.

risks.risk: The ticketing system is an unknown. On 2026-08-09 the online ticketing system returned a message stating it was currently unavailable and directing customers to the reservations office and to info@wpyr.com (c19).
risks.mitigation: That is a point-in-time observation, seen the same day by three of us independently, and it could be transient. We do not present it as a standing condition and no part of this recommendation depends on it being one. Nothing in phase one integrates with the ticketing system in either direction, which was a deliberate design choice rather than a convenience, so the build is unaffected whether that system is up, down or replaced. The one durable thing the observation tells us is that info@wpyr.com is an address your own systems point customers toward, which is part of why it is one of the three capture paths.

risks.risk: The build lands on the person it is supposed to unload. Your Reservation Agent enters reservations into the ticketing system, answers questions by phone, email and in person, and assists with train loading, passenger transfers and crossing-guard duties (c30). A new tool mid season can easily become one more thing.
risks.mitigation: Phase one adds no review step, no drafting to approve and no shadow exercise, and we killed the version of this proposal that included one for exactly this reason. The agent's day changes by one thing, weekend items arrive as a list with times attached instead of as a Monday morning surprise. The four counters fall out of the resolution they already record, so the measurement costs them nothing.

risks.risk: The union question is live. About 40 workers voted to join SMART-TD's local chapter on April 8 (c33), and the company's own response was that employees have the right to organize.
risks.mitigation: Reservation Agents are not among the roles that article names, which is why this build appears clear of it. Absence from a list is not proof of non-representation, so we treat it as a dependency to confirm in writing before anything ships rather than an assumption we quietly made for you. If Reservation Agents are inside that unit, the scope of anything touching their work is a conversation with the local before it is a deployment, and finding that out now costs nothing while finding it out at go live costs the schedule.

risks.risk: IT UNDERPERFORMS. The counters come back thin, the share of requests inside the cutoff falls under the gate, and the forfeiture conversion runs against you.
risks.mitigation: Then phase two is not funded, and we say so in writing rather than repackaging the same idea at a smaller price. The engagement ends at phase one. You keep the governed policy file, the timestamp record, the queue and the counters, all of which are yours, run without us, and continue to be worth having on their own. The whole thing is deliberately sized so that a negative result costs one pilot and one shoulder season, and so that the result is unambiguous enough to act on. Note the wider context honestly, only 12 percent of tour, activity and attraction operators actively use AI in their operations, with most still experimenting or not using it at all (c42), which is one reason we put the measurement first and the model in a later phase that has to earn its way in.

open_questions.q: What share of departures actually sells out, by departure and by date? This is the question that decides whether easier cancellation costs you money or makes you money, because it decides whether a released seat resells. Third-party travel journalism reports the popular train rides usually sell out in advance, especially during peak cruise season (c14), which is a journalist's characterisation rather than your load factors. No passenger count, no load factor and no trains-per-day figure is published anywhere. If a released seat reliably resells, this build pays for itself on that alone. If it does not, the forfeiture revenue you give up is a real cost and the case has to stand without it, which is how we have deliberately written it.
open_questions.owner: White Pass, Manager of Reservations and Sales, from your own booking data. We compute the effect either way once the figure exists, and phase one measures the conversion side of it directly regardless.

open_questions.q: Is an out-of-hours request timestamped before the 24 hour cutoff honoured at that timestamp? This is a business rule, not an engineering choice, and it is the single decision that turns this from a measurement exercise into a change in guest outcomes.
open_questions.owner: White Pass, the President, with whoever owns the cancellation policy language. Needed in writing before go live.

open_questions.q: Are Reservation Agents inside the bargaining unit that about 40 workers voted to join on April 8? The article names tour guides, announcers and workers who greet visitors as they leave their cruise ships, and Reservation Agents are not among them (c33), which is not the same thing as confirmation.
open_questions.owner: White Pass, HR/Payroll Manager, in writing before anything ships.

open_questions.q: Who administers 1-800-343-7373, and what does an out-of-hours greeting with callback capture cost to configure on that system? We have not seen the phone system, so any number we put on this today would be invented.
open_questions.owner: White Pass, plus your telephony vendor. We would rather have the vendor name and a 20 minute call than a line item nobody can defend.

open_questions.q: What actually arrives at info@wpyr.com today, in what volume, and in which languages? Your recruiting names Spanish and Japanese specifically (c31), which is evidence the need is real rather than evidence of the mix. We hold zero verbatim guest messages, because every review platform returned HTTP 403 to every attempt, so the language mix and the intent mix are assumptions until the ingest measures them.
open_questions.owner: Joint. White Pass grants access, we measure it in weeks one and two and hand you the numbers.

open_questions.q: Can your ticketing vendor expose an interface at all, and on what terms? Everything in the deferred lane, above all the self-service cancellation desk, turns entirely on this, and nobody can answer it from outside your company.
open_questions.owner: White Pass, with the ticketing vendor. Our recommendation is a written feasibility assessment in the off season before a single day of build is committed to that path.

open_questions.q: What does a forfeited fare actually cost you today in dispute handling, chargebacks and goodwill? The forfeiture clause is published (c12), the downstream handling of an unhappy guest is not, and it sits on the other side of the ledger from the forfeiture revenue itself.
open_questions.owner: White Pass, Controller, alongside Reservations. If the figure is not tracked, say so and we will leave it out of the case rather than model it.

open_questions.q: Was the ticketing system unavailability observed on 2026-08-09 transient, or is it a recurring condition? We saw it three times independently on one day (c19) and we have deliberately not built anything on top of that observation.
open_questions.owner: White Pass, whoever holds the ticketing vendor relationship. It changes nothing in phase one either way, which is why it is a question rather than a risk.
